newsitem.title: INDIA: India urged to aim for long-term oil security.
newsitem.headline: India urged to aim for long-term oil security.

text.p: India, facing a fall in domestic oil output and rising world crude prices, must aim for long-term policy measures to ensure oil security, petroleum ministry officials said on Wednesday.

Ministry officials told an economic editors conference that policy initatives were needed to meet India's oil needs since uncertainities in global prices and availability were imposing a massive burden on the nation's oil import bill.
"It is imperative that we take medium and long-term measures to provide oil security to the country on a sustainable basis," junior Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister T.R. Baalu said.

India's oil import demand of some 22-23 million tonnes of crude and 16 million tonnes of refined products cost about $6.5 billion in 1995/96 (April-March), accounting for around 20 percent to 22 percent of the country's total import bill.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told the meeting on Tuesday the country's 1996/97 (April-March) oil output was expected to dip to 32 million tonnes against an earlier estimate of 33.7 million tonnes.
He said the oil import bill for the same period was now estimated at $9.0 billion against a previously calculated $7.8 billion, due to hardening world crude prices.

Baalu said India's oil pool deficit, the amount reimbursed by the government to oil companies to make up for subsidised prices, is expected to touch 155 billion rupees ($4.34 billion) in 1996/97 (April-March) against 57 billion rupees last year.
Under the oil pool account, the government reimburses oil firms for the difference between what they pay to import crude and what domestic refiners pay them.
India's crude oil and petroleum product prices are administered by the government. Some sections including farmers and low-income groups are supplied diesel and kerosene at subsidised rates.
The government also subsidises the sale of naphtha to fertiliser plants. The plants pass on the benefits to farmers by providing cheaper fertilisers.
Baalu said the government's subsidy to the petroleum sector was also expected to rise steeply to 180 billion rupees in 1996/97 from an earlier estimate of 100 billion.
He said a revision in domestic prices of oil products would depend on the collective decision of the federal cabinet.
"As things stand I am not interested in increasing the prices. Government will take a collective view at the appropriate time," Baalu said.
The minister said demand for petroleum products was expected to rise to 81 million tonnes in 1996/97 compared to 74.7 million tonnes in 1995/96.
He said the ministry was considering a report of a government-appointed panel on restructuring the oil industry.
The panel had suggested phased deregulation of the domestic oil sector by 2002.

"There is a need to change the present fiscal regime and rationalise subsidies and price structure," Baalu said. "Market deregulation and privatisation need to be taken up in a planned and time-bound manner."

Ministry officials said to meet the rising demand of petroleum products the government had initiated short-term measures, including early production systems, deepening existing oil wells and adopting improved technology.
Baalu said other measures included evolving a new exploration licensing policy to attract greater private investment and the restructuring of state-owned oil firms.
